title: task list --across-refs coalesces per git common dir under an advisory lock (DEC-282 (a1) item 8)
description:
CARRIER from ODOC-610 / DEC-282 (a1) ADDED 2026-11-19, opum-doc, after the clock read 02:29:29Z on cont1's follow-up over opum-comm. Read BY REF from opum-doc origin/dev 68734a01 (.quest/planning.json, decision DEC-282, outcome (a1)).

Verbatim from (a1), item 8: "`task list --across-refs` coalesces like DEC-282 item 2: an advisory lock per git common directory, where a waiter whose ref hashes match a finished result reuses it."

DEC-282 item 2, which it points at, verbatim: "Coordination per git common directory (lore-cli). check and sync take an advisory lock under the clone's common git dir, so runs from different worktrees of one clone serialize instead of multiplying. A waiter whose inputs (the .quest and docs tree hashes) match a result finished while it waited reuses that result. The lock is advisory and released on exit or crash. A stale holder never blocks forever."

Ships with DEC-282 items 1-5 and 7 in the next lore/quest pair release. Depends on the per-ref cache (QCLI-563): a waiter can only reuse a result when results are keyed by the ref hashes it would have read.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A task list --across-refs run takes an advisory lock under the clone's common git directory, so runs from different worktrees of one clone serialize instead of multiplying
A waiter whose ref hashes match a result finished while it waited reuses that result rather than re-reading the refs
The lock is advisory and released on exit or crash, and a stale holder never blocks a later run forever
Tests cover the serialization, the waiter reuse and stale-holder recovery
bun run check exits 0 with the new tests included

implementationNotes:
#760 round 1 (lock half): REQUEST_CHANGES at c139a8a0f85d78260869a328a020f4a72a2d3183 from the Opus unit quest-cli-review-760, model claude-opus-5-5 (verified by the leader), review worktree review-568-c139a8a. Round 2 is in progress on the same branch (F1 port of the id-allocation .break-file shape, F2 seam test, F4, F3, F6 moot check, F8 if cheap); a fresh worktree and a new Opus unit take it. CARRIED TO THE WIRING PR, must not be missed: F5 (30 s default wait vs 60-90 s runs; a timeout must not mean run anyway) and F9 (realpath the commonDirectory; precise definition of the cache-newer-than-capture clause; the wiring catches CommonDirLockTimeoutError itself). Verdict, byte-verbatim between the relay markers:

VERDICT: REQUEST_CHANGES on opum-ai/quest-cli#760 at c139a8a0f85d78260869a328a020f4a72a2d3183. One finding blocks: the stale-recovery design does not deliver the exclusion its docblock promises. This repository has already reviewed and retired this exact rename-and-restore pattern in its own allocator lock.
Line numbers below are file lines in src/application/refs/common-dir-lock.ts (file line = diff line − 6), unless another file is named.
F1 [BLOCKING] Rename-and-restore can take the lock from a live holder. Two holders can then both run. :400-427 recoverStaleSnapshot, :438-474 restoreQuarantined.
Interleaving with three actors, using only code paths in the file: 1. A and B both read stale lock S, and both judge it stale (:216). 2. A renames S into quarantine (:406). The bytes match (:420), so A unlinks it and retries `wx`. A now holds L_A. 3. B renames lockPath into its own quarantine (:406). That file is now L_A, so the bytes do not match (:420) and B goes to restore (:425). 4. lockPath is now empty while A is live. C's `wx` at :196 succeeds, so C holds L_C. 5. B's link fails with EEXIST (:448), and B unlinks its quarantine copy. A's lock file is gone.
A and C now both believe they hold the lock. A's token-checked release correctly skips L_C, but the two runs have already overlapped.
A second failure fits in the same window without any C. If A releases during it, A's release reads ENOENT (:522) and returns. B then links A's body back. The result is an orphaned lock carrying A's live pid, which blocks every waiter until A's process exits, or for up to 10 min. In a long-lived or in-process caller that is 10 min, and every waiter's 30 s wait expires first.
The docblock at :157-165 says two recoverers "cannot both proceed to hold it". As written, that is false.
PRIOR ART IN THIS REPO: src/application/tasks/id-allocation.ts:407-418 records this design being retired after review: "A rename-and-restore, or a bare unlink, then moves or deletes a LIVE holder's lock (round 2, NEW 1)" and "no moment `lockPath` is absent while a live holder owns it (round 2, NEW 2 and NOTE 4)". The replacement is in the same file: breakers serialised through an O_EXCL `.break` file (takeBreakFile, :478-509); the lock re-read under that file and removed only if it still matches (:440-450); nothing ever parked or restored.
Fix: reuse or extract breakStaleLock/takeBreakFile, or port its shape, rather than keep a second lock primitive with the bug that one fixed.
F2 [BLOCKING with F1; test gap] No test reaches restoreQuarantined. Neither of the writer's two mutations touches it, and the two-waiter test (test :158-190) cannot open the F1 window because that needs a third contender creating mid-recovery. Proposed mutation: replace the body of restoreQuarantined with `await unlinkIfPresent(quarantinePath)`. I predict all 11 tests stay green. UNVERIFIED, since I have no shell. Whatever replaces F1 needs a seam-driven test, as id-allocation has with afterStaleJudgement/afterLockedReread.
F3 [non-blocking now, fix before wiring] The staleness rule is OR with no age floor on the pid-dead branch (:382-383). The allocator uses AND: id-allocation.ts:433-434 requires older than 30 s AND pid gone. A holder in another pid namespace (a container bind-mounting the clone) or on another host (common dir on a network share) probes ESRCH here and loses its lock at once. That also makes F1 fire more often. The reverse case: a reused pid, or a zombie that has not been reaped, reads as alive until the 10-min age clause. Recommend recording hostname in the owner, and judging a foreign host by age alone. Age compares wall clocks across processes (`now()` against `startedAt`), so an NTP step forward can steal a lock from a live holder.
F4 [non-blocking, cheap fix] A failed write leaves an empty lock that blocks everyone for 10 min. At :196-201, if `handle.writeFile` throws (ENOSPC, EIO), the error propagates and the file created by `wx` stays behind with no body. With no owner it is judged by mtime alone (:387), so everyone waits the full DEFAULT_STALE_AFTER_MS. The exit hook is not registered yet at that point, so it cannot clean up. The allocator handles this at id-allocation.ts:533-537 by closing and unlinking on a write failure. Related cases where an error leaves residue: after the rename at :406, a non-ENOENT readFile error (:415-418) or a non-whitelisted link errno (:453-461) throws with the moved lock still in quarantine. lockPath stays empty and the `.stale-<uuid>` file is left behind. Nothing ever sweeps `.stale-*` files.
F5 [non-blocking for this PR, MUST settle before wiring] The default wait timeout cannot cover the runs this lock is meant to serialise. DEFAULT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS is 30 s (:62). The ruling's context says runs take 60-90 s. If the wiring proceeds unlocked on timeout, as the error message invites at :128, every waiter after the first gives up partway through the holder's run and reads concurrently. With 4-9 runs that is the load-41 scenario again, only delayed by 30 s. Either the wait must cover a holder's run, which QCLI-563's cache may shorten, or a timeout must not mean "run anyway". This is a constant shipped in this PR, so flag it now even though nothing calls it yet.
F6 [non-blocking, needs a shell to confirm] The hardlink fallback's errno list (:453-461) has EOPNOTSUPP but not ENOTSUP. On macOS those are distinct errnos (45 and 102). If link returns one that is not in the list, the error escapes with the live lock still in quarantine. That is F4's residue, plus a displaced holder. The fallback rename (:464-473) uses POSIX rename, which replaces the target and never raises EEXIST, so the EEXIST catch at :470 is dead code. The fallback can also overwrite a third lock. The comment at :432-435 admits a residual race, but not that one. On Windows (a shipped target) the path is untested, and unlinking or renaming a file another process has open can fail with EPERM/EBUSY. Not verified. Fixing F1 the allocator's way removes this path entirely.
F7 [non-blocking; this half is sound] The exit hook (:501-510) is tidiness only, and the module says so. SIGKILL, and SIGINT/SIGTERM under default handlers, do not run it. Recovery then depends on the pid probe, which frees a SIGKILLed local holder on the next poll, with the 10-min age clause as backstop. So "a stale holder never blocks forever" does hold locally, subject to the F3 exceptions. Two minor points: each unreleased acquisition adds an `exit` listener, so a long-lived process with 11 or more open handles would emit MaxListenersExceededWarning on stderr; release does a read and then an unlink (:520-528), a small window the token check does not close. With F1 fixed it is harmless.
F8 [non-blocking; test strength] All 11 tests run in one process. Every contender shares process.pid, so the real defaultIsAlive is only ever called with a live pid. Its ESRCH branch is never exercised: each staleness test injects isAlive. The `wx` mutation proves O_EXCL is what serialises the runs, and the OS gives O_EXCL the same meaning across processes. So for the basic create path, in-process tests are fair evidence. They prove nothing about the recovery race, the exit hook, or a real crash. Ask for one two-process test: a child `bun` acquires the lock and is SIGKILLed, and the parent then acquires within a bound. The waiter-reuse test (test :295-327) checks an in-memory handshake, not the module. That is fine as a model, but it is not evidence toward AC2.
F9 [non-blocking; wiring notes] Pass the realpath'd `commonDirectory` from local-workspaces.ts:188-193, which already resolves `--git-common-dir` against the worktree. Raw output is relative in the main worktree, and :186's `mkdir(lockDir, {recursive:true})` would quietly create a stray directory under a wrong root. Consider a non-recursive mkdir of just `quest/` so a bad root fails loudly. It runs on every poll iteration, which is harmless. API shape for waiter reuse: a generic mutex with reuse inside `work()` fits 563's cache. Two caveats. The docblock's "or the cache is newer than the capture" (:233-237) needs a precise definition before wiring. And withCommonDirLock gives a caller that times out no way to fall back, so the wiring must catch CommonDirLockTimeoutError itself. The location `<common>/quest/` is shared with alloc.lock and reserved-ids, which is consistent. Permissions are the umask defaults. In a multi-user shared clone, readSnapshot's EACCES is rethrown as a hard error rather than treated as contention. That is an edge case. NOT an issue: readSnapshot reads before it stats, the reverse of the allocator's QCLI-522 order. Here that is harmless, because any mtime it picks up is equal or newer, so it errs toward not-stale.
Acceptable for an unwired primitive: F3, F6 (both moot if F1 is fixed the allocator's way), F7, F8's lack of a two-process test, F9. Must be fixed before wiring: F1 and F2 (I would fix these in this PR, because the docblock states a guarantee the code does not provide), F4 (two lines), F5 (a decision for the wiring PR). AC2 is unmet by this PR, as the writer says. AC3 is only partly met: the recovery mechanism is the part F1 breaks.
Could not verify without a shell: any test result, including my F2 mutation prediction; real cross-process behaviour, and real SIGKILL recovery; whether macOS or the /Volumes/external filesystem returns ENOTSUP or EPERM for link, and so which F6 branch production would take; Windows behaviour; Bun's process.kill(pid, 0) semantics on win32; whether `bun run check` is green at this head. F1 was derived by reading the code, not reproduced.

#760 round 2: REQUEST_CHANGES at 8190ee117110f20acf40e81fcbbe264f98059fd8 from the Opus unit quest-cli-review-760r2, model claude-opus-5-5 (verified by the leader), review worktree review-760-8190ee1. F1 is closed; one new blocker N1 (a wedged .break disables every recovery rule, the backstop included). Round 3 is pushed at 024a2b0c30830750ac4a5673900b428ef878581a (N1 both fixes, the F2 matching-path test, F8 as a real two-process test, N2-N4 folded); the round-2 red method was: the specialist backported both seams into the c139a8a0 file and ran the F1 test against it (mid-recovery create succeeded). lore-cli is porting this design under DEC-282 (a7) and takes the N1 fix too. Verdict, byte-verbatim between the relay markers:

VERDICT: REQUEST_CHANGES at 8190ee117110f20acf40e81fcbbe264f98059fd8 (opum-ai/quest-cli#760, QCLI-568, round 2)
F1 is closed. The verdict turns on item (5): a wedged `.break` turns off BOTH recovery rules, the 10-minute age backstop included. From then on every acquirer times out at 30 s and the stale lock is never cleared, which contradicts "a stale holder never blocks forever". The `.break` residual the writer inherited from id-allocation fails closed for a reason that does not apply to an advisory lock.
ROUND-1 FINDINGS
F1 (BLOCKING): CLOSED. Exactly four places can unlink the lock path, and each is guarded: common-dir-lock.ts:244-245: our own just-created file, after a failed write. :543-545: the breaker's removal, done under `.break` and only after a full-byte match against the snapshot judged stale. :597-598: release, which checks the token first. :574: the exit hook, which checks the token first. The bytes include a randomUUID token, so the byte match is stronger than id-allocation's pid+at match (id-allocation.ts:442-446). The path is empty only right after a byte-matched stale lock is unlinked, and no live holder owns it at that moment. Three-actor walk: If B1 holds `.break`, B2 gets EEXIST and returns false (:539). If B1 finishes and C creates before B2 takes `.break`, B2's re-read mismatches and it returns false (:543). Nothing is renamed, linked or restored. The imports at :3 confirm that link and rename are gone. Two breakers cannot both proceed past the re-read. The only exception is the documented check-then-unlink race when clearing a DEAD breaker's file (:509-514), and even then the byte re-read still has to match. Port fidelity: same ordering as id-allocation.ts:420-459 and :478-509. That is judge stale → seam → O_EXCL `.break` → re-read → compare → seam → unlink, then a `finally` that frees only our own `.break`. The `.break` ownership check uses the token, where id-allocation uses pid+at; that is stronger. Divergences are listed under NEW below.
F2 (BLOCKING): HALF CLOSED. In the F1 test (test:160-221), `afterStaleJudgement` replaces the lock, so the re-read at :543 mismatches and returns before `afterLockedReread` (:544) ever runs. So `expect(midRecoveryCreateSucceeded).toBe(false)` passes only because the probe never runs. On the new code it checks nothing. The check that the contender is preserved (test:218) is real, and it agrees with the writer's claim that removing byte-equality turns exactly one test red. But the "no contender can create mid-recovery" half of the title is untested. What is needed is a matching-path test: leave the lock stale, have `afterLockedReread` probe `open(wx)` and expect EEXIST, and assert the hook ran exactly once with a counter. Also, the seams do not exist at c139a8a0. The old code ignores those options, breaks the seeded stale lock normally and acquires, so it fails `toBeInstanceOf` for an unrelated reason. "Red against c139a8a0" therefore needs its method stated (were the seams backported?). As stated, it is not evidence that the test catches F1.
F3: CORRECT. The rule (:449-458) is: older than staleAfterMs → stale; otherwise at or under the floor → not stale; otherwise an unreadable owner → stale; otherwise stale only if the pid is dead. That matches id-allocation.ts:432-434, including breaking an unreadable holder on age alone once past the floor. The 10-minute backstop is a documented addition. NIT: the option doc (:103-105) says staleAfterMs is "larger than" pidGoneFloorMs, but nothing enforces it.
F4: CORRECT on the write-failure path, for both the lock (:241-247) and `.break` (:493-500), with no `.stale-*` residue. A SIGKILL mid-write now recovers after 30 s through the owner-null branch, down from 10 minutes. MINOR: if `handle.close()` throws after a successful write (:248), the file holds our live pid but no handle is returned. It stays stranded until the 10-minute backstop. id-allocation has the same shape.
F6: MOOT. No link or rename remains.
F8: PRESENT, with two MINOR problems (test:634-686): (a) Flaky ready check. The parent polls `pathExists` and then calls `JSON.parse` on the child's file. The child's `writeFile` is not atomic, so an empty read can throw. Wait for the child's "held" on stdout instead; the child already writes it and the test never reads it. (b) No real bound. `elapsed < 5000` with `waitTimeoutMs: 5000` is tautological, because a failure to recover throws before that line. Assert close to the 100 ms floor (say under 1 s) to show recovery within a bound. It does use the real `defaultIsAlive` and awaits `child.exited`, so the pid is reaped and returns ESRCH. That makes it a sound real-dead-pid test. But the child hand-writes the body and never calls `acquireCommonDirLock`, so it is not a test of two processes contending through the module.
F5, F9: deferred to the wiring PR, as agreed. Not reviewed here.
NEW FINDINGS
N1 (BLOCKING, item 5). A wedged `.break` blocks every acquisition for as long as a stale lock exists. `breakStaleLock` returns false whenever `takeBreakFile` returns null (:538-539), and the 10-minute age backstop in `isSnapshotStale` is reachable only through that same path. So a wedged `.break` turns off the backstop as well as the dead-pid rule. An empty or unreadable `.break` is never judged stale (:471). The plain answer: no single waiter blocks forever, because each one is bounded at waitTimeoutMs (30 s) and then throws CommonDirLockTimeoutError. But the stale holder is NEVER cleared. Every later across-refs call waits the full 30 s and fails to acquire until someone deletes `.break` by hand. The residual is also wider than the writer stated. A `.break` whose pid is readable and reads as alive never clears either. That covers pid reuse, and EPERM, which `defaultIsAlive` counts as alive (:393-395). `.break` has no age backstop at all, although the lock's own doc (:59-64) justifies its backstop with exactly the pid-reuse case. Why the inheritance does not carry over: id-allocation fails closed because losing serialisation there can mint duplicate ids. This module's own docblock (:17-22) says nothing correctness-critical depends on the lock. Failing open here costs at most one duplicated read. So the trade-off that justified the residual there is inverted here, and the ruling's clause is not met as written. Fixes, in either order: (a) Clear `.break` on age alone past a generous backstop (for example staleAfterMs) when its owner is unreadable or its pid reads as alive. Add a test for it. (b) Have CommonDirLockTimeoutError report the state of `.break` and the remedy, as id-allocation does (id-allocation.ts:169, :220-252). The current message (:168-171) names only the lock. Because the caller may proceed unlocked, the wedge is otherwise silent. Doing both is best. If the writer wants to keep the residual, that is a ruling question for opum-doc against DEC-282 item 2, not one for the writer or for me.
N2 (MINOR). Release is read-then-unlink (:588-598), so it can delete a successor's lock. Sequence: a holder past the 10-minute backstop reads its own token; a breaker byte-matches and unlinks; C creates; the holder's unlink then removes C's lock. The mirror order works too: the breaker re-reads, the holder releases, C creates, and the breaker unlinks C's lock. Either way the result is two concurrent holders, which means duplicated work only, since the lock is advisory. This happens only past the age backstop or with pid reuse. id-allocation's `releaseLock` (:582-584) has the same gap. The fix is in the docblock: "with breakers serialised nobody else can remove it" (:46-48) is false while the stale holder is alive. Narrow that claim and record the residual.
N3 (NIT, port divergences): (a) `readSnapshot` reads, then stats (:418-434). id-allocation stats first and documents why (id-allocation.ts:358-361). Here the mtime only matters when the owner is null, and read-then-stat can only make the age younger, so this is safe, but it is an undocumented divergence. (b) A stat or read error other than ENOENT throws out of acquire. id-allocation refuses instead (:362-368, :432). The wiring PR should decide whether an EACCES on the lock dir degrades to running unlocked. (c) `unlinkIfPresent` rethrows errors other than ENOENT inside the breaker and `finally` (:545, :551). id-allocation swallows them. (d) `name: "alloc"` resolves to `quest/alloc.lock`, which is id-allocation's lock with a different body format. Nothing reserves that name.
N4 (NIT): staleness rests on a wall clock (`startedAt` from the holder's Date.now). A backward clock step postpones every recovery rule by the size of the step. id-allocation shares this.
COULD NOT VERIFY WITHOUT A SHELL: the 16/16 local pass, and CI on this head; the claim that removing byte-equality turns exactly one test red (I traced it by reading the code, which agrees, but did not run it); the method behind "red against c139a8a0"; how often the two-process test flakes on the ready-check race; that id-allocation.ts is byte-identical (the full PR diff touches only common-dir-lock.ts and the test file, which is consistent with that, but I ran no git diff).

Verdict, byte-verbatim between the relay markers:

VERDICT: APPROVE at 024a2b0c30830750ac4a5673900b428ef878581a
(opum-ai/quest-cli#760, QCLI-568, round 3. Reviewed by reading only; I ran no tests and no git.)

"A stale holder never blocks forever" now holds on every path that waits (see (c)). None of the R3 items below blocks. The two SHOULDs are a docblock claim this round made false, and a test gap that lets two mutants of the new rule survive.

ROUND-2 FINDINGS

| finding | state | evidence |
|---|---|---|

(b) DOES AGE-ALONE `.break` CLEARING REOPEN F1?
Not the F1 window: that needed no stall. It does open a stall-gated path to the same outcome. Concrete interleaving, with a stale L0:
1. B1 judges L0 stale, takes `.break` (stamped t0), re-reads L0 and gets a match at :697.
2. B1 stalls for more than staleAfterMs before the unlink at :699 (SIGSTOP, laptop sleep, a stalled filesystem).
3. B2 judges L0 stale and gets EEXIST on `.break`. It reads B1's `.break`, finds its age over staleAfterMs, unlinks it at :668 and returns null.
4. On its next poll B2 takes `.break`, re-reads L0 and gets a match, unlinks L0, frees its own `.break`, loops and creates L2. B2 holds.
5. B1 resumes, and its :699 `unlinkIfPresent(lockPath)` deletes L2, a live holder's lock. B1 loops and creates L1.
Result: B1 and B2 both believe they hold. B2's release is safe, because the token mismatch at :758 leaves L1 alone. The cost is one duplicated ref read, which the advisory contract accepts. But it is a live holder's file removed by a breaker, and that is the case :41-42 says cannot happen. R3-1.
Second path, already present in round 2 and now reachable from an aged `.break` rather than only a dead one: two clearers both pass :662 on the same aged `.break`, and a third breaker's fresh file is unlinked by the slower clearer. Two processes then hold `.break` at once, both re-reads at :697 can match L0 before either unlinks, and the second unlink removes the first's successor. The comment at :663-667 says "the subsequent locked re-read must still match before anything is removed". That reads as protection, but it gives none once two holders exist. Folded into R3-1.

(c) DOES "A STALE HOLDER NEVER BLOCKS FOREVER" HOLD ON EVERY PATH?
Yes, on every path that waits:
- Lock with a dead pid: past pidGoneFloorMs.
- Lock with a live-looking pid: past staleAfterMs.
- Unreadable lock: by mtime, past the floor.
- `.break` with a dead pid: past breakStaleAfterMs.
- Unreadable or live-pid `.break`: past staleAfterMs.
The scenario of a fresh, unreadable `.break` that keeps being rewritten cannot happen. `.break` is only ever created by `open(wx)` (:640), which needs the previous file gone. Clearing an unreadable one needs its mtime past staleAfterMs, and nothing touches the mtime. So at most one wedge per staleAfterMs.
Two qualifications:
- A stamp in the future, from a forward clock jump that is later corrected, delays every rule by the size of the jump. That is N4, documented.
- A non-ENOENT failure does not wait; it throws. An EACCES or EISDIR on the lock or on `.break`, through readSnapshot at :520-531 via :661 or :347, ends acquire with a non-timeout error. So the clause holds here only because the code fails fast. The duty carried to the wiring PR, next to F5: treat ANY acquire error as "proceed unlocked", not only `CommonDirLockTimeoutError`. Otherwise one permission-broken `.break` fails `--across-refs` permanently.
